summary: This informational document, from the IRTF Coding for Efficient Network Communications Research Group, recommends terminology for network coding. It provides a set of terms to avoid ambiguity in future IRTF and IETF documents.

plainLanguage.summary: Network coding adds information to transmissions so receivers can recover data when packets are lost. This RFC gathers terms for discussing those techniques consistently.

subtitle: Shared terminology for network coding techniques and their building blocks.

tldr.problem: Network coding research and specifications use many related terms, which can make their meaning unclear across documents.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines shared terms for packets, symbols, coding operations, coding types, decoding, and practical signaling.
tldr.outcome: This IRTF Informational document recommends a vocabulary; it is not an Internet Standard and does not specify a particular coding protocol.

today: RFC 8406 is an IRTF Informational document published in June 2018. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC presents recommended terminology rather than a network-coding protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 8406 collects recommended terminology for network coding, the topic of work in the Coding for Efficient Network Communications Research Group. It aims to reduce ambiguity in future IRTF and IETF documents and aligns its terms with terminology used in IETF reliable multicast and forward-error-correction documents.

The RFC focuses on packet transmission and packet loss. It treats a packet-erasure channel as one where a packet is either dropped or received without error; bit-error channels and physical-layer error correction are outside its scope. It is an IRTF research-group document, not an Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives researchers and protocol designers a shared set of names for network-coding ideas. It focuses on lost packets, not on correcting errors inside a received packet.

sections.title: Packets, Symbols, and Coding Operations
sections.content:
A packet is the data unit sent across a packet-erasure channel; a symbol is a unit manipulated by encoding and decoding. A source symbol comes from the original data, while a repair symbol is produced by a coding operation. A packet can carry one or more symbols.

Encoding takes source symbols and produces encoding symbols. Recoding takes encoding symbols and produces new encoding symbols, possibly at a forwarding node. Decoding uses encoding symbols to recover source symbols. In systematic coding, source symbols are included in the output as well as repair symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets are what the network sends; symbols are the pieces a coding method combines. Encoding creates repair symbols, and decoding uses received symbols to recover original data.

sections.title: Ways to Organize Coding
sections.content:
End-to-end coding performs coding at a source and decoding at a destination without recoding at intermediate nodes. Network coding also allows intermediate forwarding nodes to recode. Coding may combine symbols from one flow or multiple flows, and it may use one path or multiple paths.

Linear coding combines input symbols using coefficients from a finite field; random linear coding chooses those coefficients randomly. Block coding divides input into blocks and processes each block independently. Sliding-window coding generates repair symbols from a changing set of source symbols. Rateless coding can generate an unlimited number of repair symbols in principle, while non-rateless coding has a predefined maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: Coding can happen only at the endpoints or also at intermediate network nodes. It can work on fixed blocks or on a moving window of data, and some methods can keep producing repair symbols as needed.

sections.title: Coding Terms Used in Practice
sections.content:
For a block code, the code rate is the number of source symbols divided by the total number of source and repair symbols. A decoding window is the set of source symbols considered together by a receiver. The rank of its payload set counts the independent equations available; a full-rank system can be decoded.

A Forward Error Correction (FEC) scheme specifies both a code and the protocol details needed to use it. It defines signaling, such as an Encoding Symbol Identifier (ESI) and FEC Payload ID, that lets encoders and decoders identify symbols and coding parameters. A repair packet may include a coding vector or enough information to reconstruct it.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver needs enough independent information to solve for the original symbols. An FEC scheme also specifies how packets identify symbols and communicate the coding information needed for decoding.
